Figure 1. Structures of the N-containing heterocycles. N-heterocycles generated by (A) previously reported bacterial CARs21,31−33 and (B) CARs

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Genome mining of bacterial CAR enzymes. (A) Sequence similarity network of A domains in identified bacterial CARs (50% sequence
identity), with sequences sharing 80% or higher identity grouped into a single node. The node size represents the number of sequences in one
node. Reported CARs are marked as black nodes, while the new Family 4 is boxed. (B) The maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree of
representative CARs with 1000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates. The colors of branches are identical to Figure 1A. (C) Sequence similarity network of
A domains in Family 4 CARs (65% sequence identity), with sequences sharing 100% identity grouped into a single node. The 5 CARs
characterized in this study are marked as black nodes.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Identification of diverse N-heterocycle natural products biosynthesized by CARs with or without other enzymes. The color-coded peaks
and boxes represent the different compound types (imidazole: purple, pyrazinone: blue, pyrazine: green, pyridine: yellow, pyrazinium: pink). (A)
Extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) of compounds 1-6 produced by P. polymyxa ATCC 842 wild-type (i, Pp WT) but not by its ΔPpCAR mutant
(ii, Pp ΔCAR) or in GSC culture medium (iii). (B) EICs of compounds 7-14 produced by B. laterosporus ATCC 9141 wild-type (i, Bl WT) but not
by its ΔBlCAR mutant (ii, Bl ΔCAR) or in LB culture medium (iii). (C) EICs of compounds 15-17 produced by B. thuringiensis serovar
huazhongensis BGSC 4BD1 wild-type (i, Bt) but not in MHB culture medium (iii). (D) Structures of the identified CAR-related natural products
determined by NMR or MS/MS. Structures elucidated by NMR are underlined. (E) The abbreviations, structures, and corresponding precursor
amino acids of the substituents appeared in this study.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Reconstruction of one-enzyme biosynthesis of N-heterocycles using in vivo and in vitro assays. The color-coded peaks in A, B, and C
indicate the various scaffolds generated (same as in Figure 3D). (A) EICs of compounds 19-22 and 6 produced in in vivo heterologous expression
system B. subtilis JH642::PlCAR (i, Bs + PlCAR), and not produced in the expression host B. subtilis JH642::control (ii). (B) Amino acid preference
screen of the five purified CAR enzymes. The measurement of enzyme reduction activity was based on the consumption amount of NADPH. The
activities of each enzyme toward different substrates were relative to the reduction on its most preferred amino acid (BtCAR with Met, BlCAR with
Trp, LfCAR with Phe, PpCAR with Val, and PlCAR with Met). (C) EICs of compounds 1, 3, 4, 6, 19-31 generated in the in vitro enzymatic
reactions containing purified PlCAR and leucine (i), methionine (ii), isoleucine (iii), or valine (iv), but not produced in control without the
substrate (v). (D) EICs of compounds 9-11, 13-15, 17, 32-38 generated in the in vitro enzymatic reactions containing purified LfCAR and tyrosine
(i), phenylalanine (ii), or tryptophan (iii), but not produced in control without the substrate (iv). (E) Detailed structure information of compounds
1, 3, 4, 6, 9-11, 13-15, 17, 19-38. The red compound numbers highlight the new CAR-catalyzed N-heterocycles in this study. The abbreviations for
the substituents are identical with those presented in Figure 3E.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. One-step biosynthesis and diversification of Nitrogen-containing heterocycles. The red compound numbers in (B) and (C) highlight the
newly identified CAR-catalyzed products in this study. The abbreviations for the substituents are identical to those presented in Figure 3E. (A)
Generation of the chemical library containing hundreds of N-heterocycles using CAR enzymes. (B) Representative N-heterocycles are generated
from two or three amino acids. EICs of compounds 39-43 produced in the heterologous expression strain B. subtilis JH642::BtCAR (i), while not
produced in the host strain B. subtilis JH642::control (ii). (C) The pyrazine skeleton with 28 possible side chain combinations. EICs of compounds
17, 35, and 45-52 produced in B. subtilis JH642::BtCAR (i), compounds 14, 27, and 53-61 produced in B. subtilis JH642::BtCAR (ii), and
compounds 4-6, 31, and 62-63 produced in B. subtilis JH642::PpCAR (iii). In contrast, none of these compounds were produced in B. subtilis
JH642::control (iv). (Chromatograms (i) and (ii) show separate extracted ion chromatograms from one LC-MS data file to clarify overlapping
peaks).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6. Screening of the CAR-generated chemical library for QS inhibitors. (A) The workflow for drug discovery bioactivity screening includes
the generation of the chemical library by CARs (i), fractionation at 1 min intervals from 15 to 40 min by HPLC (ii), identification of compounds
via LC-HRMS analysis (iii), bioactivity screening for QS inhibition (iv), and lead compounds identification (v). (B) The number and skeleton type
of identified compounds in each fraction and the QS inhibition activity of each fraction (at ∼50 μg/mL), with the lead compounds identified from
bioactive fractions.
